blocks.text: Every earlier lesson in this course quietly assumed a server could trust whoever was talking to it.
That assumption breaks the moment a server leaves your laptop, the moment a coworker points their own client at it, or the moment an autonomous agent starts calling it on someone else's behalf.
Authentication is the piece of the system that answers one plain question before anything else happens, who exactly is on the other end of this connection.
Get that question wrong and every other security control you build on top of it, permissions, audit logs, rate limits, is built on sand.
1. What Authentication Actually Answers

blocks.alt: A request is checked for valid credentials before being allowed through
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875951-341875262.png

Authentication answers exactly one question, who is making this request. It does not ask what that caller is allowed to do, that is a separate concern covered in depth in the next lesson, Authorization. It also does not ask whether the request itself looks reasonable, that is a validation concern. Authentication is purely about identity, confirming that a caller is who or what it claims to be before the server does anything else with the request.

In an MCP deployment there are three distinct kinds of caller a server might need to identify, a human user sitting at a client, a client application acting on that user's behalf, and increasingly an autonomous agent that is calling tools without a human directly present at all. A well designed authentication scheme is explicit about which of these it is actually verifying, because the three have very different trust implications.

blocks.title: A simple framing
blocks.content: Authentication answers who is calling, authorization, covered in the next topic, answers what that caller is allowed to do, the two are related but distinct questions.

blocks.text: 2. Why This Matters Even for Internal Tools
A common and dangerous instinct is to skip authentication for a server that only your own team will ever talk to, reasoning that it never leaves the office network so there is nothing to worry about.
That reasoning fails in practice for a simple reason, internal networks are not the closed rooms people imagine.

A misconfigured firewall rule, a compromised laptop on the same network, or a contractor with broader access than intended are all ordinary events, not exotic ones, and an unauthenticated internal server hands every one of them a free pass.

blocks.title: A useful rule of thumb
blocks.content: If a server can take an action that would embarrass you, cost money, or expose data when misused, it needs authentication, regardless of whether you think of it as internal or external. The network boundary is not a security boundary.

blocks.text: There is also a second reason internal tools need authentication, attribution. Even in a fully trusted environment, you still want to know which teammate or which service triggered a given action, both for debugging and for the kind of after the fact review covered later in Auditing. An unauthenticated server cannot tell one caller from another, so it cannot tell you that either.
An internal only tool still benefits from authentication, an internal network is not automatically a trusted one, and a compromised internal client should not get a free pass.
3. The Three Common MCP Authentication Approaches

blocks.alt: Bearer tokens, API keys, and OAuth are the three common authentication approaches
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875952-816246079.png
Most MCP servers settle on one of three broad approaches to authentication, each with a different balance of simplicity and capability.

API keys are a single, long lived secret string presented with every request, simple to implement and reasonable for server to server or trusted internal use, covered in full in the next module's API Keys lesson.
Bearer tokens, often JSON Web Tokens, are shorter lived, cryptographically signed, and can carry identity claims inside them without a database lookup.

OAuth is a full delegated authorization protocol, most useful when an MCP server needs to act on a user's behalf against a third party service, covered in depth in the OAuth lesson later in this module.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Best fit","Typical lifetime"],"rows":[["API key","Server to server, trusted internal tools","Long lived, manually rotated"],["Bearer token","Session based client access, first party apps","Minutes to hours, auto expiring"],["OAuth","Acting on a user's behalf against a third party","Short lived access token plus refresh token"]]}

blocks.text: None of these is universally correct, the right choice depends on who is connecting and what the server can do. A read only local tool used only by its own author has very different requirements from a remote server that can send emails on behalf of thousands of users.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Typical use"],"rows":[["API key","Simple server to server trust"],["Bearer token","Per user or per session identity"],["OAuth","Delegated access to a third party service"]]}

blocks.text: Choosing between these three usually comes down to who is calling, a trusted internal service, an individual human user, or a client acting on behalf of a user against a third party system.
4. Verifying a Bearer Token on Every Call

A common pattern for MCP servers exposed over HTTP is to require a bearer token on every incoming request, verify it before touching the requested tool or resource, and reject anything that does not check out. The verification step typically confirms the token's signature, checks that it has not expired, and extracts the identity claims the rest of the server will use.

Notice that every failure path raises a distinct, generic sounding error rather than leaking detail about why verification failed. Telling an attacker specifically that the signature was wrong versus the token was expired gives them free information about which part of their forged credential to fix next.
A malformed or missing header should be rejected the same way an invalid one is, never assume a missing credential means anonymous access is fine by default.
5. Authenticating stdio Servers Differently From Remote Servers

blocks.alt: A local stdio server is compared against a remote server for authentication
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875952-496772882.png

A local, stdio transport MCP server, the kind launched as a child process on the same machine as its client, usually does not need network authentication at all, since the operating system's process boundaries already establish who is talking to it, whoever owns the parent process. This is one reason the earlier Transport Mechanisms module treated stdio servers as comparatively low risk.

A remote, HTTP based server has none of that built in protection, any machine that can reach its network address can attempt a connection, so it must authenticate every request explicitly. This is exactly the distinction the later Secure Communication lesson returns to when it explains why encrypting the transport matters far more for a remote server than a local one, authentication and transport security tend to rise and fall together.

A locally launched stdio server often relies on the operating system process boundary itself as its trust mechanism, a remote server over the network cannot make that same assumption and needs an explicit credential.
6. Where Authentication Sits in the Request Flow

Authentication has to happen before anything else the server does with a request, before routing to a tool handler, before reading a resource, before even validating the shape of the arguments. Doing authentication late, or worse, doing it inside individual tool handlers instead of a single shared entry point, is how servers end up with one forgotten tool that quietly skips the check entirely.

Centralizing authentication as middleware that wraps every incoming request, rather than a function individual handlers remember to call, removes an entire category of accidental bypass. This same centralization idea shows up again in the Access Control lesson, where it is the natural place to also enforce per tool scoping.
Authentication should happen as early as possible in a request handling pipeline, before any tool logic runs, rejecting an unauthenticated call cheaply rather than partway through expensive work.
7. Session Level Versus Per Call Authentication

blocks.alt: Session level authentication is compared against per call authentication
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875952-660801056.png

Some MCP servers authenticate once at session creation and then trust every subsequent call on that same connection, while others re-verify a credential on every single call. Session level authentication is cheaper and fits well with the MCP session lifecycle described earlier in MCP Fundamentals, but it means a session hijacked partway through stays trusted for its full remaining lifetime.

Per call authentication, typically a short lived bearer token attached to every request, costs a little more verification work but shrinks the window an attacker gets if they intercept a single request. Remote servers handling sensitive actions generally lean toward the per call model, or at minimum a session token with a short expiry that forces frequent re-authentication.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","When it happens"],"rows":[["Session level","Once, during the initialize handshake"],["Per call","Checked again on every single request"]]}

blocks.text: Most servers combine both, a session level check at connection time to reject an obviously invalid caller quickly, and a lighter per call check afterward to confirm nothing has changed.
8. Distinguishing Client Identity From User Identity

blocks.alt: Client identity is compared against user identity
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875953-637525613.png

It is tempting to treat authenticating the client application as equivalent to authenticating the human using it, but these are genuinely different facts. A client application's identity tells a server which piece of software is connecting, while a user's identity tells it which actual person is behind that software, and a single client can be used by many different people over its lifetime.

items: Client identity answers, is this a legitimate installation of a known client application
User identity answers, which specific person is currently operating that client
Agent identity answers, which autonomous process is issuing calls with no human directly watching

blocks.text: A thorough authentication scheme keeps these three separate in its logs and its checks, since a server that can only say "an authenticated client connected" cannot answer basic accountability questions later, such as which employee's agent deleted a record.
A single client application might be used by many different end users, authenticating the client alone is not the same as knowing which specific user is behind a given request.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A single company chat application is one client, but a hundred different employees using it are a hundred different users, a server that only tracks client identity cannot tell them apart.

blocks.text: 9. Authenticating Autonomous Agents

An agent acting without a human present at the moment of the call still needs an identity, usually one derived from the human or service that configured and launched it. A common pattern is to issue the agent a scoped credential tied back to its owner, so every action the agent takes can still be traced to a responsible party even though no person clicked anything in that exact moment.

This "acting for" claim is what lets a later audit answer both halves of the accountability question, which piece of automation did this, and which human is ultimately responsible for that automation running.
An agent acting on a schedule, with no human present to type a password, typically authenticates with a long lived credential scoped as narrowly as possible to just the actions it actually needs.

blocks.title: A practical pattern
blocks.content: Give a long-running agent its own dedicated credential, separate from any human user, so its activity can be tracked, scoped, and revoked independently.

blocks.text: 10. Failing Closed When Authentication Cannot Be Completed

blocks.alt: An incomplete authentication check fails closed rather than letting the request through
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875953-605603643.png

Authentication logic occasionally encounters ambiguous situations, a token verification service that is temporarily unreachable, a malformed credential that does not cleanly parse, a clock skew that makes an expiry check uncertain. The safe default in every one of these cases is to fail closed, reject the request, rather than fail open and let it through because the check could not be completed cleanly.

blocks.title: Fail closed, not open
blocks.content: A server that lets requests through when its authentication check errors out has effectively made an outage in its identity provider equivalent to disabling authentication entirely. Reject on any doubt.

blocks.text: If a server cannot verify a caller identity for any reason, a dropped connection, a corrupted token, the safe default is always to reject the request rather than silently allowing it through.

This fail closed default sometimes costs a small amount of availability, an occasional legitimate request rejected due to a transient verification hiccup, but that tradeoff is almost always worth it compared to the alternative.
11. Logging Every Authentication Event

Every authentication attempt, successful or not, is worth recording, who or what attempted to connect, whether it succeeded, and a timestamp. This is a narrow slice of the broader auditing practice covered in full in the final lesson of this module, but it deserves specific mention here because authentication failures are often the very first visible sign of a credential leak or a brute force attempt.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Why it matters"],"rows":[["timestamp","Establishes a timeline for incident review"],["subject claimed","What identity the credential asserted"],["result","Whether the attempt succeeded or failed"],["source","Network origin or client identifier of the attempt"]]}

blocks.text: Recording every successful and failed authentication attempt, covered in depth in the Auditing lesson later in this module, is often the first signal that something has gone wrong.
A sudden spike in failed authentication attempts is often the earliest warning sign of a credential being guessed or brute forced against a server.
12. Authentication Is Not Authorization

blocks.alt: Authentication confirms identity while authorization decides what is allowed
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439875953-811229106.png

It is worth stating plainly, since it is one of the most common points of confusion, that confirming a caller's identity says nothing at all about what that caller should be permitted to do. A perfectly valid, successfully authenticated credential can still belong to someone who should not be allowed to delete a database or read another user's data.

Keeping these two checks structurally separate, one function that establishes identity and a distinct one that decides permission, is what makes a server's security logic reviewable. The very next lesson, Authorization, picks up exactly where this one leaves off and covers that second check in full.
A successfully authenticated caller has proven who they are, that alone says nothing yet about what they are permitted to do, the next lesson covers exactly that distinction in depth.
13. Rotating and Revoking Credentials

Any authentication scheme needs a plan for what happens when a credential needs to stop working before its natural expiry, an employee leaves, a laptop is lost, a token is suspected to have leaked. Long lived credentials like API keys need an explicit revocation list or rotation process, while short lived tokens shrink this problem automatically simply by expiring soon on their own.

This is exactly the trade off explored in depth in the API Keys lesson later in this module, long lived secrets are simpler to issue but harder to revoke quickly, while short lived tokens require more infrastructure but limit how long a leaked credential stays dangerous.

code.content:
# revoking a leaked key immediately
token_store.revoke("sk-leaked-key-123")
# any call using that key now fails verification instantly

blocks.text: A credential that can never be rotated without downtime tends to get rotated far less often than it should, building rotation in from day one keeps this a routine task rather than an emergency one.
Worked Example

Imagine a remote MCP server that exposes internal customer support tools to a small team, look up a ticket, add an internal note, and escalate a case. The team decides every request must carry a short lived bearer token issued when a support agent logs into the company's identity provider, rather than a single shared key everyone uses.

When a support agent leaves the company, their identity provider account is disabled centrally, which means their tokens stop verifying almost immediately, no separate MCP specific revocation step is needed. This is the practical payoff of choosing short lived, centrally issued tokens over a long lived shared secret for a server handling real customer data.

code.content:
token = request.headers.get("authorization")
identity = verify_token(token)
print("authenticated as", identity)

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Skipping authentication for a server because it is "only internal", when internal networks are routinely less isolated than assumed
Authenticating inside individual tool handlers instead of one shared entry point, leaving a gap the moment someone adds a new tool and forgets the check
Returning detailed error messages that tell a failed caller exactly which part of their credential was wrong
Failing open when a token verification service is temporarily unreachable
Treating a successfully authenticated request as automatically authorized to do anything
Using one shared long lived credential for an entire team instead of individually issued, individually revocable ones

blocks.text: Practice
Take an MCP server you have access to, or a small example server you build for this exercise, and add a single shared authentication middleware function that runs before every request is dispatched.
Have it check for a bearer token, reject with a generic error message on any failure, and log both successes and failures with a timestamp and claimed subject.

Then deliberately send a request with a missing token, an expired token, and a token with a corrupted signature, and confirm all three are rejected the same way from the caller's point of view even though your internal logs correctly distinguish them.
Try sketching what your authentication check would need to log to make a security review, months later, able to answer exactly who accessed what and when.
Key Takeaway

Authentication is the single question every other security control in an MCP deployment depends on, who exactly is making this request. Get it wrong, skip it because a server feels internal, or let it fail open under pressure, and every permission check, audit log, and access control rule built on top of it is only as trustworthy as that first, weakest link.
Once a caller's identity is established with confidence, the natural next question is what that caller should actually be allowed to do, which is exactly where the next lesson, Authorization, begins.
Keep in mind that a strong authentication scheme with a weak authorization model still leaves a system exposed, knowing exactly who is calling is only half of building an MCP server people can trust.
